items.title: "This cast of perfected future characters" was built 190 lines back
items.where: Using hindsight to « re-do » memories of trauma in a healthier way, P1
items.my_version: Now, once you’ve got this cast of perfected future characters (from Borrow Hindsight) in your mind, you can also go back to earlier traumatic memories and relive them in a better way. For example, I’ll take one instance from my own childhood. I was only spanked one time as a child. I hung up the (expensive) phone call my dad was on with a very important official in another country, because I wanted some attention. I don’t think he was exactly furious at me, but he decided this deserved a spanking, even if he didn’t agree with spanking in general. Since he wasn’t furious, the spanking didn’t really hurt, but it hurt me emotionally quite a lot, because I was so extremely shocked that my parents would use physical violence on me. Like I lost my sense of safety with them at that moment. And I may have learned that I was undeserving of attention, that I behaved in ways that made me deserve physical violence, that I was bad, etc.

items.title: Re-evaluation Counseling is explained at its second mention
items.where: Use Childhood Photographs Gently, P6
items.my_version:
Put the photo back in its drawer when you’re finished. If it starts tugging at you, so you keep going back to search it or you need to know for sure, or you’re getting overwhelmed, take a break from it right then. Settle yourself in the present to close out properly. Re-evaluation Counseling, a global movement of peer counseling, always ends on this “Present Time” reminder. Can be as simple and silly as “Oh, Today is Monday, my favorite day of the week!”

The avoidant guard shows up when you get close to some painful memory or insight. Suddenly you’d rather have a drink, check your phone, or do anything aside from directly feeling it (even a yawn can come with an “I’m so done with this” feeling). Maybe this guard doesn’t believe there’s a grown-up around who could handle what’s coming? That yawn might actually be the opposite of checking out, though. Re-evaluation Counseling counts yawning as productive emotional discharge, a feeling on its way out.

items.title: "Pl/ork" is spelled out 790 lines after you coin it
items.where: Understanding Reparenting, P4
items.my_version:
Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding a better Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate and might feel difficult. Many struggle to get past the silly, awkward feeling of it. Over time, instead of shying way from the silly, we can use the silly feeling in the work, to make it more playful. I call it pl/ork (play + work) ! With time, the adult/child roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

Your little one wants to play, too, which is why I call the deeper therapy pl/ork. Many times we adults see things as work that a child would see as play, like yoga, for example. So if it feels like you’re enforcing everything as a discipline, see if you can change that discipline into a game. Personally, I can really get a lot of enjoyment when I feel those lovely stretches without thinking it’s another task. A lot of the best discoveries come when you’re both just messing around, kind of like how kids tell you what’s really going on from the back seat, when nobody’s looking right at them. Play not only paves the way for therapy, but is a part of how successful therapy should be measured.

items.title: "The dog kind of love": the dog paragraph went missing
items.where: Ask God for a Loan, P1
items.my_version: Sometimes it’s not that you can’t love in general. Your dog can chew up your good shoes and be forgiven before you’ve found the other one. But maybe you direct that love to your little one and the attempt goes flat, or starts to feel weirdly unsafe. Just feel that love you can feel for others for a minute, in your body, before you try to redirect anything. Then as you relax into that and enjoy it more, imagine it flowing downhill, like an overflowing river of delicious chocolate. Now imagine how happy your inner child is at the bottom of the hill to play in that chocolate love that rolled down!

items.title: Typos in Understanding Reparenting (7)
items.where: Understanding Reparenting, P4
items.my_version:
Reparenting means consciously evolving and molding a better Inner Adult inside you, comprising a loving Nurturer, a safe Adult Protector (hereafter just the Protector) and a wise Guide. This chosen Inner Adult super hero gets into a real, loving relationship with the little one you still carry. That grown-up notices the old patterns and practices better ways of responding. At first, it’s deliberate and might feel difficult. Many struggle to get past the silly, awkward feeling of it. Over time, instead of shying away from the silly, we can use the silly feeling in the work, to make it more playful. I call it pl/ork ! With time, the adult/child roles become second nature, so you spend less of your life managing yourself and more of it living with purpose, loving, relaxing, and playing.

And I realized that it doesn’t make sense to ask the child to « heal itself, » which is really a disguised request for the child to abandon its own nature and turn into an adult. I call that “forced adulthood,” where the child has to deal with situations the evolved inner adult should be handling--we see this in actual children all the time when their parents are not providing care. People even wear t-shirts saying, “I don’t wanna adult today.” The forced adulting often goes along with a misperception that there is something wrong with the inner child. Instead, we need to separately develop the qualities of a good inner parent for that rightly vulnerable child: the loving Nurturer, safe Protector, and wise Guide.

The Guide is the one people misunderstand the most, because a lot of the bad parenting or misdirection we originally received was likely lacking in Protector and Nurturer functions, while over-relying on harsh guidance. So I left it out of the first version of this framework until my friend Key pointed it out as crucial. Without a healed Inner Guide, our lives can become small and like a never-ending therapy session when we focus only on caring for ourselves rather than giving ourselves a mission as well. That’s the Guide’s job. But on the other hand, some people over-rely on their discipline or their mission to avoid caring for themselves. And many folks try to find an ideal guide via some kind of guru-led political or religious cult.

Forced adulthood : You’re still stuck identifying as the lost inner child, forced frequently into handling situations that require more maturity, even if it looks like you’ve got it all together. At this stage, use your childlike superpowers to come into the “Wow of Now” (have you seen the movie Waking Life?), and make sure there’s enough safety around you to continue with reparenting.

Whichever stage you’re at, saying the right thing when you sit down with your little one helps, but you also have to start actually doing some of it in the rest of your life. Depending on your maladaptive patterns, improvements could look opposite to each other. If you’re a workaholic normally, then your little one might start believing in grown-up you when they catch you lying down because you’re wiped out, instead of pushing through one more chore. Or the opposite, when you stop procrastinating so much and clean your room, then they start believing in you.

But even though my depression was gone, the sending-love-outward metta practice didn’t reach everything in me. An old childhood wound could still hit, like if someone accused me of being lazy, and then suddenly it’s like I was that same little kid again, even tho the spiritual part of me felt free as a bird. And a lot of the childhood stuff around my attachment to girls/women was still there.

items.title: Typos in Safety and Readiness (4)
items.where: Dip Your Toes In Before You Go Deep, P1
items.my_version:
How much of the grown-up you is actually here right now? Check if you can pause before you act. Are you following through after making decisions? If you can’t do those things because you’re basically still stuck identifying as the frightened kid, then let’s leave the deeper conversation until later. Do whatever helps you come back a bit before you try to talk to little you. And have someone steady there to support you if possible.

This part tends to scare the wrong people, like somebody who’s horrified by their own thoughts. Everybody gets scary thoughts they’d rather not have sometimes, and they don’t make you a bad person, but why would you bring your inner child into the middle of them? The nice thing about inner child therapy is that you can wait until you’re calm and actually ready. A real parent doesn’t get to do that, which is one reason nobody manages to get a perfect 4.0 GPA on the parent report-card their children bring home. 😛

My father used to tell suicidal people, “Oh, you want to kill yourself? That’s wonderful! Now you can change what you’ve always been too afraid to change in your life, and then see if you still want to end it!” So, what would you tell my dad? What’s the change you still can’t bring yourself to make? Leaving a relationship or quitting a job? Telling your family who you really are? Those might sound difficult, but they’re actually considerably easier and more likely to help than dying.

items.title: Typos in Building Your Inner Adult (18)
items.where: Borrow the Adult To Become the Adult, P1
items.my_version:
Now, don’t tell anyone about this ! I’m going to reveal my Magician’s Secret. I call it the « borrowed adulthood trick ». The new grown-up you’re moulding can start outside your head, as someone who likes you just the way you are, or as something you do to protect your little sweetie pie, like letting the phone ring when you know already how that call goes. You don’t have to pretend to feel anything to let a phone ring. It may take many such ignored calls before your inner child can start trusting you (and all the while, the parent you inherited calls your efforts fake).

Even Pema Chödrön (who inspired parts of this guide), who comes from a tradition where devotion to a guru is a big deal, still says a teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up.

Some gurus really do demand surrender, and they’re the opposite of the Guide: they point you at themselves for everything, as if they want to be your God. Others are so professional that they don’t even need to ask anyone to follow them. Someone seems to get your little one like nobody ever has, or treats it like it’s special, and it starts thinking, “They know me better than I know myself ! Can you believe it ?” 🙊 I still remember a Sadhguru video where he said anyone who follows him is an idiot, and his followers were still worshipping him in the comments, proud idiots. 🤪

A complete ideal parent may be impossible to imagine (unless you saw The Brady Bunch). And imagination is pretty hard for adults anyway since it kinda gets stamped out of kids at an early age (along with spirituality), but it’s not just a foolish waste of time. It’s actually a genius mode unlock. So since the adult is actually a baby when it comes to power to imagine, start small: Borrow one capacity at a time from a figure who embodies it well.

While all of these super powers should be developed alongside each other, the inner child’s receptivity will naturally follow this order : first he/she wants to feel safe (Protector), then, building on that safety, feel loved (Nurturer), and then building on the safety & love, trust allows the little one to be eager to take guidance, and that’s where Guide-building comes.

One of my favorite teachers, Mr. Rogers, gave us an excellent example of how to extract the sweet nectar of truth from what less advanced souls might recoil at. In the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood, Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, “I can’t imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father.” He doesn’t collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what’s worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest “genuinely tested” him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he’s very proud of both his sons. Then he says, “But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn’t have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective.”

When your little one says “I don’t trust you,” you can answer, “I believe you. And I love you.” I learned this when I was 5. My mom told me it was time for bed (or something equally outrageous to a 5-year-old). I cried and screamed “I HATE YOU! I wish you were dead !” 😡 She answered, “But I love you!” 🥰

When it’s your little one yelling at you, though, try not to turn “But I love you” into a prompted line you say on cue, because then it can feel like a tactical ruse to brush the anger off. Your little one will be watching to see if the love stays afterward and takes whatever’s true in their anger seriously.

Your little one might say it’s you, without giving more details at first. Keep practicing your listening, and eventually you’ll get more of a concrete complaint, which you can consider without getting flustered from the meanness they packaged it in. Like my anger at bedtime, their swearing is there to get them heard, so once your ear guards are off, they don’t need it anymore.

Maybe just imagining a caring grown-up makes you feel more threatened, or lonelier. Lonelier is a strange one, with somebody right there. Then go smaller still, to the least cruel response a decent adult could offer your little one. This method of finding the most feasible next challenge is called scaffolding.

Taking the hostility out makes room for warmth. Sometimes the warmth is actually there, with a cold part standing in front of it. If you’ve never been safe being loved, your ego can act like a rigid security guard that won’t let the feeling in. But it generally will stand down once it feels its concerns have been heard and addressed. But the guard is still available for dealing with people who haven’t earned your trust.

When a good friend sits with you while you fall apart it does help you feel better. You call them again the next time, and they get a little better at it every time while you don’t. So steal some of it. Usually what helped was how they just sat there without trying to fix you. Ten seconds of sitting with yourself like that is good enough for a start, so try it before you call next time.

If you don’t have anyone like that right now, try remembering when you did. Perhaps a therapist or your grandmother really cared for you. Think of someone like that you remember fondly, and imagine how they would sit beside your little one.

Borrow Your Love For Someone Else

Notice how, when you offer thanks (to the universe, to life, to God, whatever you may believe in), a space in your heart opens up. It might not feel immediately like you suddenly know the real meaning of Divine Love, but it’s a little spark of … something.... There’s a tiny bit of freedom, of peace, stillness, softness. And as that softness deepens each time, you start to understand what I mean by Divine Love. Many people have written books on this topic (like A. Helwa’s book, Secrets of Divine Love, for example). I hope you are able to experience this when you try it out for a while, and I’d really love to know how it works for you!

Once you start to feel that lovely softness of the heart (which can become a very deep field of « perfect freedom »), invite your little one in with you as your spiritual integration practice. They might go numb, or call BS on that. If so, they might just need to see if you’re actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection, be patient, and be open to the possibility that your Higher View is missing the trees for the forest. If you instead retreat back into your cozy corner, it’s the food bank feast all over again: You can have an enormous spiritual feast upstairs while the child is still starving downstairs.

Another Sufi teacher, Hazrat Inayat Khan, wrote, “God breaks the heart again and again and again until it stays open.”

items.title: Typos in Practicing With Your Little One (6)
items.where: Use Childhood Photographs Gently, P2
items.my_version:
While you look, notice any new feelings or urges, and any tightness or unusual feelings in your body, including the good ones. Use Pema Chödrön’s “feather touch” approach to gently bring some light and love to the edges of any contracted feelings. Is there something that younger you seems to want you to understand? Some of it you’ll remember yourself, and some of it you might even glean from talking to family/friends from then (“You hated that coat”). It might just be an inference you’re guessing from the picture, or perhaps it triggers an image or a dream. Or just nothing comes up. Ask what your little one needs from you now, and do a bit of it.

We don’t need to ask it leading questions, like “Who abused me & how?” or “What memory is my body hiding?” Grilling one photo until a story shows up is a good way to get a story, but stories aren’t necessarily the truth, and even if they are accurate, the feelings beneath them are still more important. Memory is an amorphous thing, easily influenced by guided imagery and suggestions. Look at this study, for example, where people were shown a doctored photo of a childhood hot-air balloon ride they never took. Half of them actually started sorta remembering it. I’m sure you can relate.

For some people, writing might make them feel more confused, especially at first, or nothing might want to be written. Then just keep track for a while, and save the patterns for later, if they turn out to matter at all.

When journaling, you might be surprised sometimes by the myriad things that come into your mind seemingly out of nowhere. Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you’re in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your little one asking.

Anxiety is often a part of you that’s trying to protect you, making a guess about what’s coming, like that people will laugh at you. Sometimes it’s right, sometimes it’s useful, sometimes it’s not. Anxiety is not necessarily bad by itself, but as they say, the fear of fear is worse than the fear itself. Hearing it out and taking any action that seems legitimately beneficial as a result, often helps it to pass.

Without an ending, the processing can just start looping. So when you’re done, look around and say where you are. Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair under you, and remind yourself about something silly and obvious, like what century Pharaoh Tutankhamun was crowned (1332 BCE in case you forgot!)…

items.title: Typos in Discovering and Healing Old Patterns (3)
items.where: “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”, P1
items.my_version:
My ex, Xandria, taught me to append “And so that’s the way it happened!” to a difficult memory. Say it the way a grandpa would finish a story on the porch. (“Once upon a time…” helps if the start is where you get stuck.) Somehow it moves the whole thing out of the courtroom, where the case was still being argued, and into your life story. Pick a memory you can handle for the first few tries.

Healing does need to get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can’t be put on a schedule. If someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground. And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury.

« Hurt people hurt people, healed people heal people » means that hurt people pass on pain they never worked through, although « externalizers » are the ones who directly hurt others, while « internalizers » try to protect others by holding that « secret burning thread » inside themself, which ends up exploding onto others anyway at times when it gets to be too much to hold. You may have heard this story from somebody telling you to forgive, and it sounded like they must have no clue how deep the betrayal was. When you see it for yourself, though, you might find yourself forgiving them, and if you’ve held them uniquely to blame, the rage can soften into something more accurate.

items.title: Typos in When the Practice Gets Difficult (2)
items.where: For some people it only stops feeling fake in an altered state, P1
items.my_version:
Like on MDMA or deep in meditation. All of a sudden your little one is right there! Oh my gosh! And the love or grief that sounded like therapy talk is just obvious. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened. I’d still hang on to that connection you felt, even once it’s gone, and try to bring a little of it into your normal life. You’ve felt that your little one is real now, so talking to them afterward isn’t just pretending. If you’re « lucky », it’s not a question of trying to maintain that connection, but trying to figure out how to deal with the rawness of it after the high wears off. items.title: Typos in Bringing Reparenting Into Real Life (11)
items.where: Play Is Part of the Work, P3
items.my_version:
A lot of what adults tend to lose, your little one still has, like the silliness and the irreverence, the rawness, the creativity, all that, and maybe a connection to the Great Mystery from before your karma ran over my dogma 🤪. That’s the spark of life they bring, and you get to draw on it and give back, so it’s more communion than command. For one example of the spark, there’s my post Treasuring the Inner Child’s Gift.

But that spark of life might have been suppressed as you grew up.

If your childhood meant avoiding pain and keeping the people you needed close, your attention got used up reading danger (was that sigh about me?) and meeting their expectations, and when curiosity or mistakes got you punished, or it felt like they loved you less, you got better at playing the « chameleon ».

So early on, the practice is finding out who’s actually in there, through long reflection with no outside input, and journaling just for yourself, without picturing a reader. Time alone in nature helps too, and so does getting back the preferences that got buried: the foods you really like and what feels good to do, and what you believe and feel when nobody’s around to take your cues from. Focusing (Eugene Gendlin’s method of listening to a vague, felt sense in your body) can especially help you notice feelings and preferences the part you’ve been playing learned to overlook. Any words you put to them can stay tentative (“I hate cooking... or just for everybody?”) while you look at what they seem to mean and revise how you read them.

As you tell the part you’ve been playing apart from the authentic self that didn’t get much practice, notice whether it makes you more curious about both, and better able to relate to them. Or does it have you thinking, “That chameleon’s fake, and I’m getting rid of it”? Keep in mind the chameleon was a skillset that somehow worked to help you fit in. Even if you’re not planning on playing James Bond anytime soon, you still might need to smooth your edges out sometimes as part of socializing. You can’t always disagree with everyone on everything and still expect to be enjoyable/enjoy company.

Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--“First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable.

It’s often in handling conflict that we see the real inner child jump out. So if you’ve been wondering where they are in a session, here you go, let’s pl/ork !

When you miss someone, let the ache be a cue for love. It doesn’t have to become one more problem to solve, and pushing it away won’t help. If love’s there, “I miss you” becomes “I love you.” Or there’s the loving-kindness wish: “May you be loving, peaceful, and free.” You can picture them. Or don’t, and just feel the care going their way.

The best licensed, listed therapists you’ll find that come close will be doing Internal Family Systems (IFS), or Schema Therapy. I’ll talk more about those in the appendix. Open Path Collective (or a similar resource in your country) lists thousands of affordable therapists. You can filter them by Schema or IFS. You can often find even more Schema therapists at the official site.

I’ve tried all the top AI therapy apps, and they’re all pretty bad. I’m trying to make my own based on this guide, but I’m becoming more convinced that unsupervised AI therapy is just a toss up. That doesn’t mean you can’t get a lot of great insights sometimes when talking to AI, but just expect it to go sideways sometimes, and don’t let it replace real humans who love you and want to think with you. Actually, I find one of the best uses for it is to improve my interactions with real people. For example, it can help me formulate more careful replies to people who are too sensitive to take my excessive bluntness or wry humor (although I wouldn’t send them actual AI text).

items.title: Typos in Conclusion and Appendix (10)
items.where: You Are Worthy of Love. Always., P1
items.my_version:
And the love you’re worthy of is the same love as back in « Your Loan is PRE-APPROVED! », the Divine Love that can start as a little spark of relief when you give thanks. That kind, whether you’d say it comes from God or the universe itself or your subconscious, was there before you could earn anything. Love from a person is more conditional than that. Somebody’s love running out on you still says nothing about what you’re worth.

My reparenting guide is part of the larger reparenting and inner child therapy category. As far as I can tell, it was first developed in 1976 by Dr. Lucia Capacchione. Although Lucia is no longer with us, [her institute still trains therapists] (https://luciac.com/instructors.php) in her methods (including art therapy and other things). I greatly respect and appreciate what Lucia has given us to work with. While there are many inner child therapy offshoots (often less codified than Lucia’s book, Recovery of Your Inner Child), it would be impossible for me to compare my guide to each individual therapist’s approach. Below are the differences between Lucia’s approach and my guide’s approach :

Of the scientifically studied clinical approaches I know, Schema Therapy, developed in the 1980s-1990s by Jeffrey E. Young, is the closest to this guide. Its therapists do what they call limited reparenting: within professional limits, they give you some of what a good parent would, with warmth and firmness and some playfulness too. Over time you take that in, and it becomes your own “Healthy Adult,” who looks after your “Vulnerable Child” and stands up to the punishing parent in your head. The healthy adult recognizes when a need differs from the strategy you use to meet it, and it helps you set limits. And it gets on with adult life, like work and the things you’ve committed to. All that sounds like my Nurturer, Protector and Guide by other names, and since the therapist’s version becomes yours bit by bit, it’s borrowed adulthood too.

Being all scientific and stuff does have its drawbacks also. Schema Therapy’s name pretty much tells you all you need to know. What the heck is a Schema anyway ? It’s normally described as a « pervasive pattern of thinking, feeling, and behaving » (learned in childhood). Although I find a slightly different definition of it from Cleveland Clinic : « A schema is a long-lasting outlook or assumption that you have about yourself, others or the world. » But yeah, put those together and that’s basically what it’s talking about. So the schema therapist takes answers from a questionnaire you fill out and maps your difficulties onto a set list of 18 schemas, which themselves map onto a set of modes, like the Vulnerable Child or the Punitive Parent. Based on those schemas and modes, the therapist assumes some things about your childhood that would explain them.

Internal Family Systems (IFS)

Is a perfect Higher/True Self already waiting in there to be your guide or parent? I’d call that claim [spiritual bypassing] (bypassing.u-dont-exist.com). I’ve experienced that Higher Self perspective myself, though, in very powerful meditations. For example, one time, while still married to my first wife Ann, who was becoming more violent and crazy as time went on, we got super high on weed and we were both in some higher realm as our higher selves. My higher self asked her higher self, « Are you going to keep getting more and more crazy ? » Her higher self said, « Yes. » It was like we could see the whole timeline of life from above. Although, my friends already told me the same thing, quite sober. 😅

I’m also not a fan of the strange and complex cast of characters in IFS. IFS splits up my « inner child » into an indefinite number of wounded young parts called “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. And the parts just keep coming: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... At some point it’s a maze, and as my friend Pink, who has been healing her Dissociative Identity Disorder, explained, while it can be useful to have validation of the parts that one experiences, and ideas for how to work with them, it can also get overwhelming. People who are already overwhelmed can thus become more split up than before. I’ve seen many others echo this same evaluation, and it makes sense to me.
